description:
Our team brings together experience in artificial intelligence, machine learning and full-stack development. 

Our project work covers space and aerospace problems. It includes a PCA-optimised SVM model that classifies solar flare intensity and a Kalman filter for aircraft height estimation. We have also built a 3D AI avatar for virtual meetings. We work in Python, JavaScript, React, Node.js and TensorFlow, and we bring that mix to ASTRA-MIND. We combine data analysis, intelligent systems.
summary:
ASTRA-MIND is a prototype health monitoring platform for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It tracks five domains: cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, immune, behavioral and radiation. A FastAPI backend and SQLite database store every measurement with a data-provenance tag, and a live dashboard shows current values and trends.

It addresses the challenge in four ways:

It learns each astronaut’s personal baseline instead of relying on population thresholds.
It flags deviations and links alerts that appear across several domains at once.
It forecasts the next 24 hours with a stated uncertainty range.
It summarises overall status as a digital twin score.

It keeps working through communication outages. Data and alerts queue onboard, then sync to an Earth-side view once the link returns.

This matters because crews on deep-space missions will face delayed contact and limited medical support, so early, personalised, offline-capable monitoring could help catch problems sooner.

All data here is synthetic, and the scores show deviation from baseline, not diagnoses. They need medical review.
details:
What it does and how it works

ASTRA-MIND is a prototype that monitors an astronaut’s health on a long mission. It simulates ten signals across five domains: cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, immune, behavioral and radiation. A live dashboard shows current values, trends and alerts.

  1. Data: a generator produces hourly synthetic readings for each crew member, including slower periodic assessments such as blood markers.
  2. Storage: a FastAPI backend saves every raw measurement in SQLite with a provenance tag (SYNTHETIC) and a synced flag.
  3. Baseline: each person’s normal range is learned from their first 72 hours.
  4. Alerts: readings far from that baseline are flagged. When several domains deviate together, a combined cross-domain alert lists the supporting observations.
  5. Forecast: a 24-hour projection comes with a 90% uncertainty range.
  6. Digital twin: a score per domain and overall summarises current status.
  7. Offline mode: during a simulated communications outage, monitoring continues onboard and data queues locally. After reconnection the queue syncs to the Earth-side view.

Benefits

  • Alerts are personalised, so each astronaut is compared with their own normal instead of population thresholds.
  • Monitoring does not depend on a live link to Earth.
  • Alerts come with the observations behind them, so they are explainable.
  • Raw data is preserved and labelled by origin.

Intended impact

The aim is to help flight surgeons and crews notice health drift sooner on missions where medical support and communication are limited. It is a decision-support concept, not a diagnostic tool.

Tools and technology

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML and CSS.
  • Backend: FastAPI with Uvicorn, and SQLite.
  • Frontend: a plain browser dashboard with hand-drawn SVG charts and no external libraries.
  • Statistics: median and MAD baselines, robust z-scores, and Holt damped-trend forecasting.
  • Testing: pytest, with 3 passing tests.
  • Hardware: only an ordinary computer. There are no real sensors, because all data is simulated.

What is creative about it

  • It joins three ideas in one lightweight tool: personal baselines, cross-domain alert linking, and a single digital twin status score.
  • The offline-first design treats a communications blackout as the normal case.
  • Every data point carries its provenance, so simulated and real data can never be confused.

Factors considered

  • Safety: scores are deviations from baseline, not disease probabilities, and nothing is presented as a diagnosis. Medical review is required.
  • Honesty about data: everything is clearly labelled synthetic.
  • Resource limits: it uses simple statistical methods that run anywhere, even without internet, instead of large models.
  • Demonstrability: injected events and a communications outage button let the system be shown end to end.
  • Known gaps: Isolation Forest, Chronos-2, a medical assistant with retrieval over NASA documents, and a React frontend are planned but not built.
